Emitting only 39 decibels, this infrared heater features quiet air circulation that moves the heat through large spaces. We tested it in a 200-square-foot office, and this space heater made quick work of warming it. Infrared heaters don’t heat the air; instead, they heat objects. This heater’s quiet fan made it feel like the heat permeated farther and made a difference in overall room temperature.

It’s also packed with features including standby, eco, low, and high power modes. The digital display shows the thermostat’s setting, which makes it easy to make adjustments based on comfort levels.

We’re big fans of remote controls. This model’s remote control allowed us to make comfort adjustments without getting out of our office chair. We appreciated that we could leave it on all day while we worked, and it would turn on and off as needed. There’s also an adjustable timer, which can go up to 12 hours before automatically shutting off the heater.

Overall, it’s a nice-looking heater that can handle spaces up to about 850 square feet. It’s not the most mobile unit, weighing 24 pounds, but it does have casters for easier mobility.

Get the Dr. Infrared Heater space heater at Amazon, Lowe’s, The Home Depot, Walmart, or Dr. Heater.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4/5; Performance 4/5; Noise 5/5; Portability 5/5; Value 4/5

Figuring out the heat in a finished basement can be an ordeal but might be easily solved with the De’Longhi SlimStyle digital convection panel heater. This model can be set on the floor or mounted on the wall (the latter being best for basement duty), and it produces up to 1,500 watts of heating power. It measures 21.8 inches tall (with feet) by 32.2 inches wide by 8.5 inches deep.

The De’Longhi features a convection-style design that is virtually silent in three out of the four modes, and a fourth mode with a fan to help pump out the heat. It also features a fifth mode (anti-freeze), which the manufacturer says kicks on when the temperature in the space reaches 41 degrees Fahrenheit; this is to help prevent frozen pipes. The heater has a built-in tip-over switch as well as an overheat sensor, timers, and an electronic digital display. Unfortunately, it doesn’t come with a remote.

We’re not relegating the De’Longhi to the basement because it’s ugly; we honestly found it very nice looking. However, we think it’s best there for its included wall-mount brackets and the fact that it has a freeze-protection mode (ours activated at 45 degrees, not 41 like the manufacturer stated). With so many pipes and mechanicals in a finished basement, we thought this was the perfect solution to protect the investment. Also, most space heaters don’t reach settings that low, so this one works really well for that purpose.

There is one thing we couldn’t figure out, however: Why in the world doesn’t it come with a remote?

Get the De’Longhi SlimStyle space heater at Amazon.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 5/5; Performance 5/5; Noise 5/5; Portability 4/5; Value 4/5

The Heat Storm Logan Deluxe infrared heater is all about coziness. This powerful space heater features a 1,500W output, a digital display, and a remote control for managing the device from the couch. It has a faux-wood box-style design with fabric-covered sides, allowing it to blend in with comfortable living room decor. It can also handle large living rooms, considering it can warm up to 1,000 square feet.

This model features several modes—including high, medium, low, and auto—that control the heater based on the preset temperature. It also has a safe-touch exterior that remains cool and safe, a child lock, and overheat protection. The heater operates quietly (measured at 46 decibels on a sound meter app from about 4 feet away) as well. It measures 15.3 inches tall (with wheels) by 12.3 inches wide by 10.8 inches deep.

We’ll be honest and say that this heater has to match a living room decor to be a perfect fit, but if one of the three finish color options works, the unit can sit in the corner of any room and blend in until it’s needed.

While it’s light (10 pounds), the box itself is simply faux wood, which doesn’t seem as high in quality as other real-wood heaters that we’ve tested in the past. It had a better digital display than any of those other box-style heaters, however, and it produced a lot of heat, bringing a 63 degree Fahrenheit living room to 70 degrees Fahrenheit in about 15 minutes. Also, for those who care, it blows hot air out at the perfect height for one of our old dogs, who instantly laid down in front of it and fell asleep. We assume other four-legged friends will love it, too.

Get the Heat Storm Logan space heater at Amazon.

This space heater performed well in many respects. It has an adjustable thermostat, 11 heat settings, a cool-touch exterior, and a compact design. What it doesn’t have is an automatic tilt shut-off feature. That means if it gets knocked over, it keeps running. In a home with pets, kids, and, honestly, most adults, it could keep running face down, posing a fire hazard. For that reason, it didn’t make our list of top picks.

We tested these space heaters in person, in real-world situations. They were all tested in a home office setting where the office was 150 to 200 square feet in size. One of the test offices also had large windows, so the room temperature fluctuated more often. We tried them on different surfaces, from plush carpet to bare floors.

For models with a digital display, we set the thermostat between 70 and 75 degrees Fahrenheit to see how well the space heater kept a consistent room temperature. From there, we made adjustments to settings (low and high), timers, and safety features. For example, we tipped over every single space heater to make sure it turned off.

Models designed to turn on and off based on the thermostat were left running to see how they performed over time. Some stayed in standby mode for hours without turning on because a furnace kept the room at temperature. We wanted to make sure they wouldn’t turn on if it wasn’t necessary. Ease of use was also a consideration, and models with remote controls or intuitive designs got higher marks from us.

Besides taking into account the size of the room you’re planning to heat, Saidov says it’s a good idea to “find a model that has a set temperature.” She adds, “This will ensure that the unit doesn’t overheat the space.” She also says to make sure the space heater is Underwriters Laboratories (UL) certified, a third-party certification that means the heater meets certain safety standards. And, most importantly, “Electric space heaters should always be plugged into a wall outlet and grounded. Using extension cords and power strips can be a fire hazard.”

A small space heater might be suitable under a desk or next to a lounge chair, but it likely won’t make a dent in a sizable chilly room. A space heater’s size should suit the room that it will warm and should, of course, be as safe as possible.

For those just starting to shop, it might come as a surprise to find so many different types of heaters from which to choose. Each type has its pros and cons, and not all space heaters are suitable for all rooms and situations.

Fan space heaters function by heating the air around an electric coil or wire elements and then dispersing the heat with a fan. They are among the least expensive models but do not offer the same efficiency as other types. Therefore, fan heaters are best suited to rooms without drafts or for warming a small space quickly.

Convection space heaters warm air over ceramic plates or disks and allow it to radiate warmth into the room. Some models do include fans for quicker heat dispersal and, like conventional fan heaters, they work best in rooms without drafts. Convection heaters come in compact or tower models, often with exterior cases that are cooler to the touch. Prices vary depending on wattage and added features.

Infrared space heaters are among the quietest options for the home. They generate heat quickly by radiating heat to the objects—including people—in front of them. As opposed to heating the air in the room, this type of heater heats the user, making it a good choice for use in drafty rooms. All that’s needed is for the user to aim it directly at where they’re sitting.

Oil-filled space heaters (another type of radiant heater) are also a quiet option. Because they are capable of putting off an abundance of heat while using less electricity than fan-type models, these heaters are well suited to larger rooms. Due to the weight of the oil and the steel casing, these heaters are relatively heavy, but many come with wheels to make relocating easier. Oil-filled space heaters take a while to heat up, but they radiate continuously once they do.

Micathermic space heaters combine convection and radiant heating processes. Designed as a panel to stand or hang on a wall like a piece of artwork, they create a welcoming ambience for the senses by mimicking the look of a real fire and radiating heat. Some models include fans for greater efficiency and remote controls for extra convenience. These advanced heaters vary widely in price.

Space heaters are a leading cause of house fires, so the best space heaters boast safety features to reduce risk. Manufacturers have introduced automatic shutoffs that kick in when a unit overheats or gets inadvertently knocked over. In addition, many have exterior cases that keep units cool to the touch at all times. Some models even come equipped with motion sensors that automatically turn the heater off when a pet or child comes too close. For extra peace of mind when purchasing, look for the letters NRTL on the space heater packaging, which indicates that the model has been tested for safety by the Nationally Recognized Testing Laboratory.

As a general rule of thumb, select a space heater that will produce 10 watts of power for every square foot. For instance, to heat a 12-foot-long by 10-foot-wide room, a shopper would need to purchase a 1,200W space heater. A very large room may require more than one space heater to maintain a comfortable temperature throughout.

Other factors that affect a space heater’s efficiency include ceiling height, the insulating factor of the exterior walls, the number of windows, and the available outlets. While high-wattage heaters offer more heat than lower-wattage models, they’re limited to the capacity of the electrical outlet; a home’s standard 110-volt electrical outlet can only provide 1,500W of power, so that must be the wattage cap for any machine plugged into it.

One of the main reasons for using a space heater is to save on energy costs. But unlike many other appliances, space heaters do not require energy testing by the Environmental Protection Agency, nor does the agency issue Energy Star ratings for them, so those who are serious about saving will want to opt for the most efficient type.

Oil-filled space heaters are among the most efficient because they heat the oil and the metal casing, gradually dispersing radiant warmth into the room. Once the oil reaches the desired temperature, less energy is needed to maintain that temperature. Even after an oil-filled heater is turned off, it will continue to radiate heat for up to 30 minutes or more. Next in energy efficiency are infrared space heaters, which use up to 10 percent less energy than space heaters with coils and fans.

For the most part, space heaters are among the quietest of all small appliances. Space heaters that use radiant heat, either infrared or oil-filled, make virtually no noise. Traditional space heaters with fans will emit an average of 35 to 45 decibels of sound, approximately the same as soft indoor conversation (which could be suitable to use as a white noise machine).

Homeowners and renters can save on utility costs by using a space heater in one or more rooms rather than heating the entire home. For the toastiest—and safest—results, check out these useful tips.

Most space heaters should be turned off at night and when you leave a room. The exception is an oil-filled radiating space heater, which can be left on. However, make certain not to leave anything flammable within 3 feet of the radiator.

Oil-filled radiant heaters use the least amount of electricity because once they heat up, it takes very little energy to keep them warm. Plus, they will radiate heat for up to 30 minutes or more after they’ve been turned off.

The safest space heater is one that will automatically shut off if it overheats or if it accidentally tips over.

#7860. Why Do Construction Barricades Come in Different Colors? The Colors Decoded

Red, yellow, and orange barricades don't always mean the same thing. Learn what common safety colors signal and when to stay clear.

Yellow caution tape is a pretty familiar sight, whether it’s blocking off a wet floor or keeping people out of a construction area. Orange barriers along the highway and red warning signs at job sites are just as common. But barricade colors aren’t random, and they don’t all mean the same thing.

In the U.S., OSHA has rules for certain workplace safety colors, while ANSI provides guidelines for signs and warning tape. Road construction follows a different set of standards. Depending on the location, the same color might serve a different purpose.

Learn what the most common barricade colors mean, where people are likely to see them, and what to watch out for.

There’s a reason red is a common choice for warning signs. OSHA uses it to identify danger, emergency stops, and fire protection equipment. At a construction site, a red “Danger” sign might warn of exposed electrical equipment or another hazard that could cause serious injury. OSHA’s general-industry rules also call for red warning lights at barricades and temporary obstructions.

Of all the safety colors, yellow might be the one people see most often. It shows up on caution tape, warning signs, and around areas where crews are working. OSHA uses yellow to warn of physical hazards, including falls and falling objects. A damaged walkway or an area undergoing maintenance might have yellow tape around it.

There’s no shortage of orange around construction sites. On workplace warning signs, the color often identifies hazards that could cause serious injury, particularly around machinery or equipment undergoing repairs. Orange also makes road construction easier to spot. Crews use orange barriers and signs to warn drivers about upcoming work, lane changes, or other temporary traffic conditions.

Instead of warning people away from something, it usually helps them find safety equipment. A green sign might point toward a first aid station, identify emergency equipment, or provide instructions for workers. It’s especially useful in workplaces where people need to find these resources quickly.

Blue signs typically provide information about workplace equipment or procedures that don’t directly involve a hazard. For example, a blue notice might explain that a machine is temporarily out of service. Unlike red or yellow warnings, blue notices generally provide information rather than warn of immediate danger.

Purple isn’t a color people encounter very often on construction barricades, but it does have a specific safety use. OSHA requires certain radiation warning signs to feature the familiar radiation symbol in purple or magenta against a yellow background. These signs warn people about radiation hazards, including areas where access may be restricted.

Those orange-and-white striped barricades lining roads and highways aren’t quite the same as the warning signs used inside workplaces. The Federal Highway Administration has separate rules for these barriers, which crews use to close lanes, block roads, and direct traffic around construction.

There’s also a purpose behind the diagonal stripes. When a barricade directs drivers around an obstruction, the stripes slope down toward the side where traffic should pass.

OSHA, “29 CFR 1910.144, Safety Color Code for Marking Physical Hazards” OSHA, “29 CFR 1926.200, Accident Prevention Signs and Tags” ANSI, “Z535.1-2022: Standard for Safety Colors” ANSI, “Z535.5-2022: Safety Tags and Barricade Tapes” OSHA, “29 CFR 1910.1096, Ionizing Radiation” FHWA, “Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices, 11th Edition with Revision 1”

#7859. Arkansas Bar Official Allegedly Transferred Points from Some Bar Examinees to Others

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From the Arkansas Supreme Court Thursday:

Evidence exists that Givens harvested points from a number of examinees' scores and then added them to other examinees' scores within the same test administration. Thus, she unilaterally elevated some examinees' scores to the minimum passing score of 270 or greater. Brech also identified at least one instance in which score alterations may have reduced an examinee's score-who otherwise would have passed-to a failing score. And in at least one instance, the individual who should have received the top score on the Arkansas Bar Examination had their score reduced thereby naming another examinee as the recipient of the highest score on the exam. If these allegations are true, these actions constitute an unprecedented breach of public trust.

An internal review by Robert Brech, Executive Director of the Supreme Court of Arkansas's Office of Professional Conduct and Programs, has uncovered extensive irregularities involving the Court's Office of Professional Programs and the administration of the Arkansas Bar Examination. The matter was turned over to state and federal authorities.

As of today, the Prosecuting Attorney's Office for the Sixth Judicial District filed formal criminal charges against Nancie Givens for 65 counts of tampering with a public record under Arkansas Code Annotated section 5-54-121 in connection with the alleged altering of numerous Arkansas Bar Examination scores and the deletion of files purportedly intended to conceal that misconduct. The charges followed a criminal investigation initiated in April 2026 by the Arkansas State Police and the Federal Bureau of Investigation. As always, all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty in a court of law.

Moving forward, we are committed to holding those involved accountable, taking continued corrective oversight of the Arkansas Bar Examination, and determining the appropriate course of action.

In February 2026, Givens, the former Executive Director of this Court's Office of Professional Programs, resigned. At that time, Robert Brech was serving as Executive Director of the Court's Office of Professional Conduct. Following Givens's resignation, the Court directed Brech to supervise the Office of Professional Programs, which oversees the administration of the Arkansas Bar Examination.

Upon his review of the Office of Professional Programs' records and administrative operations, Brech discovered that a large number of files and electronic communications were modified or deleted in early January 2026. Approximately 11,400 files were deleted or rendered unavailable. Most of those files included Arkansas Bar examinee applications, profiles, and examination score sheets that the Office of Professional Programs was required by this Court's rules to retain for twenty-five years.

Brech immediately notified a member of this Court, who directed him to determine the extent of the missing records and identify any other irregularities. On the basis of his review of the remaining files, Brech identified numerous discrepancies involving Arkansas Bar Examination scores across at least eight test administrations between July 2020 and July 2025. At that time, the matter was referred to the appropriate state and federal authorities.

Evidence exists that Givens harvested points from a number of examinees' scores and then added them to other examinees' scores within the same test administration. Thus, she unilaterally elevated some examinees' scores to the minimum passing score of 270 or greater. Brech also identified at least one instance in which score alterations may have reduced an examinee's score-who otherwise would have passed-to a failing score. And in at least one instance, the individual who should have received the top score on the Arkansas Bar Examination had their score reduced thereby naming another examinee as the recipient of the highest score on the exam. If these allegations are true, these actions constitute an unprecedented breach of public trust.

The vast majority of examinees who were previously informed that they had passed the Arkansas Bar Examination by the Office of Professional Programs did, in fact, pass the exam. Those examinees affected will be notified by the Office of Professional Conduct as soon as possible upon definitive confirmation of their status.

The Court is working with state and federal authorities to recover deleted and missing data, analyze all test administrations within that time frame, and determine the full scope of this grave and potentially criminal abuse of power. The people of Arkansas deserve, and the Court is committed to providing, total transparency in this matter. However, further disclosure will be forthcoming in a manner so as to not compromise the ongoing state and federal criminal investigations. Accordingly, additional disclosures will be limited as those efforts remain underway.

As an immediate step, independent of any state or federal criminal investigation or prosecution, Nancie Givens has been referred to the Office of Professional Conduct for investigation of extensive violations of the Arkansas Rules of Professional Conduct. See Ark. R. Prof. Conduct 8.1(a) & 8.4(a)-(e). Furthermore, new testing procedures and security measures were implemented with the February 2026 administration of the Arkansas Bar Examination to ensure systemic accountability and safeguard the integrity of the examination.

We recognize the profound consequences for affected examinees, the Bar, and the public at large. Our paramount concern is safeguarding litigants, the integrity of the legal profession, and public confidence in the administration of justice. While these matters remain under criminal and administrative investigation, we commit to pursue continued corrective measures in an effort to reestablish confidence in our institution.

#7857. 6 Cool Ways to Decorate With Battery-Operated Candles, From Now Until the New Year

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Published Nov 6, 2026 10:58 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

As November rolls around and people bring out their holiday décor, many choose to display candles to cultivate a warm, inviting atmosphere throughout the holiday season. Candles can brighten a room, shift the mood, provide soothing scents, and offer a pop of color. However, some homeowners shy away from using open-flame candles because they come with a fire safety hazard.

Battery-operated candles provide a great alternative to traditional candles that are aesthetically pleasing, says Kanika Bakshi Khurana, principal interior designer and founder of Kanika Design in San Mateo, California. “In addition to providing a less hazardous option for displaying during holidays, battery-operated candles provide a practical solution for those who may be too busy with other activities,” explains Khurana. Also, they don’t leave soot or wax on surfaces like traditional candles do, and you save money from not having to continually purchase replacement candles once they burn down completely. “The added feature of being able to control how long each candle is lit through timers and remote controls provides additional convenience in using these types of candles,” she adds.

Here are several battery-operated candle ideas for decorating your home this winter season.

Operated by an intelligent remote control, these realistic flameless candles use a new technology to simulatef real flickering candles.

Battery-operated candles can be used to safely illuminate items displayed on your fireplace mantel. Khurana recommends creating a layering of candles on the mantel by using multiple battery-operated candles of varying heights and combining them with assorted décor items, such as greenery, pine cones, or branches for an element of depth in the winter design. “When using flames that have a gentle flicker, you will find this candle arrangement to be more visually appealing, particularly when lit at night,” she says.

Bookshelves and built-in cabinets—and the items displayed on them like framed pictures and sculptures—are often stunning during the daylight hours but offer no visual interest when darkness falls. Khurana suggests placing small, battery-operated candles inside decorative glass vases or on open shelves with your books and ceramics. “The light will create a warm ambiance for the area and make the surrounding objects appear as if they are illuminated,” she explains. And with battery-operated candles, you won’t be stuck trying to get candle wax out of your vase or jar the next day.

Set up a safe, inviting environment for guests by displaying battery-operated candles instead of open-flame candles in windows and throughout your entryway. “An entryway can be one of the first areas in your home where you use battery-operated candles to set the tone for when people enter your house,” says Khurana. “It is easy to arrange two or three flameless candle pillars on a console table with some other objects, a small seasonal flower arrangement, and a decorative mirror, which will help reflect the light created by the candles and enhance the welcoming atmosphere.”

Flameless tapers and other types of candles are perfect for creating that warm, candlelight vibe at your holiday dinner table, while providing peace of mind for you and your family as they dine with you, says Khurana. “Place each taper into a vintage brass holder (mixing high and low) down the middle of your holiday dining table and add a simple arrangement of fresh greenery and/or seasonal fruits to create a stunning holiday centerpiece.”

Using battery operated candles, you can create a warm and cozy atmosphere in your bedroom without setting an actual candle near your bedding or curtains, notes Khurana. She suggests placing two of these small candles together on a dresser or beside a photo frame on a nightstand and adding a vase between them. “This will help you slowly shift from being awake during the day to being relaxed at night,” she says.

Flameless candles also look fabulous inside lanterns, which come in a wide variety of sizes, materials, and colors. “A couple ways I have used this idea is to place a large lantern next to a fireplace or to group two lanterns of varying sizes together at the base of an entryway console,” says Khurana. “To create a more elegant look for your lanterns, you can choose from antique brass, black metal, or natural wood options, and instead of using bright and cool-toned light bulbs, use warm white candle lights.” For out-of-reach spots, you can even choose remote-controlled flameless candles for easy operation.

#7856. Bonfire Season Is Here — Here Are the Dos and Don’ts for Staying Safe

How to not to expose yourself to toxic fumes, burn down the neighborhood and injure the kiddos, plus other tips for enjoying a stress-free bonfire.

Cool fall evenings naturally put our minds on the merits of bones-warming bonfires. And while many create cherished family memories and set the backdrop for festive community events, some end up in tragedy, with emergency room visits and property damage.

“Every season there are always the same preventable mistakes made that lead to injuries,” says attorney Kevin Henrichson. “Falling into the fire, using gasoline, adding fuel when you shouldn’t, failing to supervise children and consuming alcohol all raise the stakes of something bad happening.”

Ahead, experts walk through exactly what to do and not to do to stay safe while enjoying a bonfire.

Notify your local fire department of your plans and ask them for guidance concerning:

“One phone call to the fire marshal’s office takes two minutes,” says fire and home safety expert Eugene Klimaszewski. “Otherwise, the consequence of burning without a permit on a restricted day is a fine, and if it gets away from you, it’s your liability.”

Look for a flat, open spot away from fences, barns, houses, trees and ground vegetation. The National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) recommends keeping bonfires at least 25 feet from the house and other structures.

“That number isn’t arbitrary,” says Klimaszewski. “Radiant heat and drifting embers are what ignite a deck railing, a vinyl fence or the mulch bed against the house. Every ember that lands on a roof or in a gutter full of dry leaves is a coin flip. Most go out. The one that doesn’t becomes a structure fire.”

Build the fire downwind of your home and close all windows and doors on the fire side, to prevent smoke from getting in.

“Even a small amount of smoke reaching an indoor smoke detector is enough to set it off,” says Klimaszewski. If you have a monitoring system, that could trigger a call to the fire department. “At best that’s an embarrassing conversation with the engine company. In towns that charge for repeat false alarms, that’s a bill on top of the embarrassment,” he says.

Pro-tip: If you have an older home, which isn’t airtight, put your alarm system on test mode or notify your monitoring company about your bonfire plans.

Wind can carry embers up to a mile, which means a bonfire on a windy day can easily end with a wildfire or house fire. If your planned bonfire day turns out to be windy, reschedule it. And even if there isn’t a breeze, plan for one by clearing all debris from around the fire pit and building rocks or bricks up higher on the windy side, which protects the fire from the wind plus radiates heat toward you for extra warmth.

Kiln-dried wood is the best. Seasoned hardwoods like oak, cedar and hickory are particularly good because they burn cleaner, longer and hotter than soft woods like pine and aspen (though a little soft wood kindling makes starting a fire a lot easier).

Steer clear of gasoline or other accelerants, as they too often lead to burn injuries, out-of-control fires and noxious fumes. (One year, my neighbor used so much gasoline to start a bonfire that the resulting shock wave from the explosion knocked pictures off of people’s walls three blocks away).

“A lot of people think they can use gas or lighter fluid to get the fire started or revive it, but please never do that because the vapors can flash back and get everyone nearby,” says Henrichson. “Gasoline is particularly dangerous and should never be used to start or revive a fire.”

Pro-tip: If you struggling to start a fire, build up a good kindling base and use a campfire starter or small bit of tightly twisted newspaper. Ample kindling will help you get a hot coal-bed established, which will burn larger logs more effectively plus lessen smoke.

Avoid newspaper, cardboard and other paper products, which tend to break down into large flying embers. Also, never burn anything with adhesives, plastics and other chemicals. The health risks of this are obvious, but plastics and chemicals are hiding in many items you might not realize, including: dryer lint, food packaging with shiny ink, glossy magazines, pressed woods including butcher block, varnished furniture and clothing made with synthetic fibers.

Before lighting the fire, set up a water source in case embers become a problem. That will also make it easier to put it out completely when you’re done. NFPA actually requires a hose, bucket or extinguisher be on hand for all recreational fires, and for fires to be attended at all times.

“A fire that’s left alone for ten minutes while everyone goes inside for more drinks is the one that ends up on the local news,” says Klimaszewski. “And an unattended fire that spreads is the homeowner’s liability, full stop.”

Assign someone to supervise the flames at all times to prevent the fire from getting out of control, and to keep kids and pets from standing too close. Equip the supervisor with proper protective clothing, including a fire-resistant glove, long-handled poker tool, shovel, closed-toe shoes and eye protection.

“The most common injuries I’ve seen are from people falling into the fire, and young children are vulnerable to this because they may want to play in the area where everyone is hanging out by the fire,” says Henrichson. “There should be a no-enter zone that is explained to children every single time, and the person tending the fire should not have any alcohol.”

Watch for loose sleeves, blankets, boots and other combustibles that are too close to the fire. “Those fun marshmallow-roasting memories are great to make, but shaking a burning marshmallow can cause trouble, and if you use metal skewers, they can burn you too,” says Henrichson.

Also, know what to do beforehand if something ends up catching fire. “The old advice that we were told years ago is still true: stop, drop, and roll if your clothes catch fire,” says Henrichson. “Repeat this as necessary every time kids approach, because they don’t always know to stay back.”

Embers can easily reignite hours or even days later, so the best practice for putting out a bonfire is to drown it, stir the ashes, and then drown it again until everything is cold to the touch. Don’t cover embers with dirt, as that actually insulates them, leaving open the possibility for them to reignite if they’re uncovered by a stiff wind.

Pro-tip: Put ashes in a metal container with a lid, on a non-combustible surface, away from the house, garage and deck for several days before they go in the trash, says Klimaszewski. Never put them in a plastic bin or next to the house.

#7855. 6 Tricks to Get Back Into Your House After Getting Locked Out

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Updated Nov 6, 2026 11:53 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Q: Last night I was almost locked out of the house, as I nearly left my keys on the counter before walking to a neighborhood BBQ. That got me thinking—what should I have done if I locked myself out of my house? And are there steps I can take to make sure it never happens? I’m thinking of giving a spare key to a neighbor, but I’m unsure what else can be done!

A: Getting locked out of your house can be a frustrating experience, but it’s not as uncommon as you may think. And unless you’re prepared, the situation can be more terrifying than it has to be.

Thankfully, there are plenty of ways to get back inside a house without breaking in through your door, even if all signs point to the opposite. From checking windows or removing door knobs to calling a locksmith or family member with a spare key, there’s no shortage of options at your disposal. Once you get back inside, you can then take steps to protect yourself from getting locked out again. This includes installing smart locks or hiding a key in a secure location somewhere else on your property.

If your door lock is locked and you’re outside the home, the first thing to do is stay calm. It’s easy to panic, but there are several ways to remedy the situation. Here’s a look at actions you can take to get back inside.

The quickest way to get back inside a home when locked out of the house with no key is by searching for another door or window that may be unlocked. Whether it’s a back door or basement window, be sure to check all entryways that are reasonably accessible. This might mean removing or damaging a window screen, but if it’s the difference between being locked outside and getting back inside, that’s a small price to pay. If there’s no easy way to get to the second-story windows, it’s best to leave them be—there are plenty of other ways to get inside, so there’s no reason to risk an injury.

If a family member, friend, or neighbor has a spare key, now is the time to try and contact them. People locked out of their homes who still have their smartphones with them can place a quick call to the owner of their spare. If the cell phone is inside the house, consider asking a neighbor or walking to a local shop and using their phone. This won’t be possible in all locations (especially in rural areas), but it’s a nice backup if a smartphone isn’t readily available. At any rate, contacting the person responsible for the spare key should be a top priority.

Individuals locked out of a rental unit can contact either their landlord or the maintenance company to help get back inside. The landlord will almost certainly have a spare key. If the rental unit is part of a large apartment building, there’s likely a maintenance technician on site who can help instead of the landlord. Many apartments also have a leasing office, so if someone is locked out of an apartment and doesn’t have the contact details for maintenance or their landlord, they can try this location as a backup. Most leasing offices are staffed during normal business hours and are more than willing to help tenants locked outside their apartments.

Though it’s not easy, attempting to pick the lock is worth consideration. Some door latches can be reached with a twisted paper clip or credit card. To attempt this, the card or paper clip needs to slip past the strike plate and catch the door latch. Once the latch is caught, it can be pushed out of place and the door can be opened. If the deadbolt is in place, this technique will not work. But if it’s just a simple latch on a door knob, it’s certainly worth a try. Unlocking a door this way is tricky, though it may be effective in some situations.

Another possible way to get back inside is to remove the door knob. This requires users to have access to a standard toolkit, though often just a screwdriver can get the job done. Most knobs don’t have exposed screws on their exterior plate, but it’s possible to gain access to them by looking for a small slot somewhere else on its faceplate. This small slot keeps the knob and faceplate in place—by depressing it, users can remove the faceplate and gain access to the screws.

With the screws exposed, they can be loosened and the door knob can be removed. This gives access to the lock’s inner workings, part of which includes a mechanism for opening the door. Try using a screwdriver to twist the inner component, which should unlock the latch. Keep in mind these general steps won’t work for all types of locks, as each model is unique. For detailed steps, it’s a good idea to look up installation instructions for the specific brand in question.

The simplest way to unlock a locked door is by contacting a locksmith. These trained professionals can not only circumvent a locked door, but they’re trained to also repair or replace the lock once the door is open. The process typically doesn’t take very long, with many home lockout services lasting no more than an hour.

Pricing for locksmiths varies by location, but in an emergency situation, they’re worth every penny. Many locksmiths deal with more than just residential homes, making them a great choice when locked out of a car, RV, or any other building. They can even rekey a lock and help people locked out with the key stuck in the door. They are also trained to assist with changing locks on the door if an upgrade or replacement is required. So if none of the above steps work, a locksmith offering house lockout service is the best option.

While accidents can happen to anyone, there are steps people can take to prevent future house lockouts. This includes simple things like hiding a spare key somewhere around the property and giving a spare to a neighbor, along with more complicated tasks like installing smart locks. Not all of these steps will apply to all homes, but the more failsafes in place, the better the odds of getting back inside.

Installing one of the best security systems (such as Vivint or ADT) is a great way to keep burglars at bay and improve home security. If the system also includes a smart lock, users have a quick way to get back inside when locked out. In fact, many smart locks are designed in a way that makes it nearly impossible to get locked out, as they can be controlled with a physical key or the built-in keypad.

With a traditional lock, leaving the key inside the home results in a lockout. With a smart lock, leaving the key inside simply means users need to use their digital code to get back inside. Some of the best smart locks, like the Yale Assure Lock 2, also work with mobile companion apps, letting users open the door with their smartphone.

Alternatively, many of the best electronic door locks toe the line between traditional and smart locks, making them a good choice for homes looking for the best of both worlds. It’s important to read up on what smart locks are before making a purchase, as well as learn about the types of door locks available, as there are advantages and disadvantages to them all.

While shopping for a security system and smart lock, homeowners can also pick up other security gear, including the best door security bars to help prevent break-ins.

Giving a key to a trusted neighbor or nearby family member is a simple (yet effective) way to prevent getting locked out. Ideally, this will be someone easy to reach and within walking distance of the home, ensuring they can quickly get to the home without requiring a phone call or a long drive.

However, it’s important to have complete trust in the person receiving the spare key. Not only can they help during lockouts, but they can essentially enter the home whenever they’d like. This makes it important to only pass out spare keys to neighbors who have proven themselves to be responsible and trustworthy. Otherwise, this step could result in more headaches than it’s worth.

Hiding a spare key on the property is another popular way to ensure lockouts never happen, but this needs to be handled with care. Ideally, a lock box with a spare key inside will be installed near the front door, allowing only people with the password access to the spare. This is leagues better than simply hiding a key under the doormat or inside a yard decoration, as anyone who stumbles upon the key will be able to get into the home.

If a lockbox isn’t used, then ensure that the hidden spare key is in a location that won’t be disturbed by harsh weather or easily seen by prying eyes. This includes inside a dog house, under a brick or patio paver, inside a magnetic holder placed under a bench, or stowed away inside a fake rock. Poor locations to hide a key include under a doormat, under a flowerpot, or on top of the door frame.

Keeping a spare key in a wallet or purse comes with serious drawbacks. For one, if the wallet or purse is lost, someone will now have a key to the home, meaning it’s best to have the lock rekeyed. If the key is placed in a purse or wallet without a way to keep it secure, it’s also possible for it to slip out while reaching for a credit card or cash. Because of this, anyone storing a key in their wallet or purse will need to invest in a key holder—these are cheap, secure, and prevent the key from rubbing against the wall of the wallet and piercing its side.

The benefits of keeping a spare key in a wallet or purse may outweigh the drawbacks, especially for people who never leave home without their purse or wallet. This essentially gives individuals another way to get back inside their home without requiring their keychain.

The simplest way to prevent a lockout is to get in the habit of never leaving home without a set of keys. This is easier said than done, but certain actions help turn this into a routine. Many people prefer to place a dish or tray near their front door for valuables like their keys. When leaving the home, having the keys right next to the exit makes it virtually impossible to forget them. Other people like to use a keychain that’s visually appealing, ensuring it catches their eyes when leaving the home.

Aside from making the keys easy to spot when leaving, good habits include reserving a specific pocket for keys, checking for keys before closing any lockable door, and communicating with family members or roommates to ensure they don’t get locked out if no one else is home.

Getting locked out of the house can be a frightening experience. Thankfully, there are several ways to remedy the situation and get back inside. From asking a neighbor for a spare and checking for unlocked windows to calling a locksmith or attempting to pick the lock, there’s an option that works for everyone.

The best option is to prevent lockouts from happening in the first place. To that end, installing smart locks and stashing a spare key on the property are both great options. Each home will have techniques that work better than others, and it’s up to each individual to determine what works best for them.

#7854. I Thought I Wanted a Single-Family Home. Turns Out, I Missed the Rental Income

We thought we wanted a single-family home, but adding an ADU made it the perfect place for us.

I’ve always had benchmarks for knowing when I’ve “made it” in life: a car with power windows and locks, a refrigerator with a water dispenser and owning a single-family home. The last one stems from the fact that my wife and I always owned two-family homes. We lived in one unit and rented out the other for over a decade before we finally had the means to move into a single-family home.

But the funny thing was, when we finally got there, something was missing. Our single-family home didn’t feel as rewarding as I thought it would. Ahead, I share why this long-sought-after dream house didn’t quite feel like one and how a new Massachusetts law allowed us to add the missing piece to our family’s forever home.

After 10 years of renting, my wife and I wanted to buy a home. We decided on a two-family property because we were nervous about taking on too much financially. A single-family home seemed like a luxury that was out of reach, but the rental income from a two-family home made homeownership seem feasible and financially safe. Collecting that first rent check was an amazing feeling, and it cut our mortgage payment in half. We were hooked. Being landlords wasn’t always stress-free, but regular rental income gave us so much financial freedom.

Seven years later, we moved into another two-family home that better suited our growing family and kept the first one, too. We continued to work and save for another five years. As we approached 40, buying a single-family home felt like the next logical step. It was the ultimate end goal, right? So we bought a single-family fixer-upper in a nice neighborhood and started making repairs. Our kids settled into a new school district, and we made friends with the neighbors.

At first, it all felt great, but living in a single-family home wasn’t everything we’d hoped it would be. Mostly, we found we really missed the rental income we were used to in our two-family homes. It felt foolish to have a house that only took money out of our bank account without putting any back in. We didn’t want to move, and soaring home prices made buying another property out of the question. To find ways to generate income from our property, I tried renting out our in-ground pool, second garage, and backyard to dog owners. None of those ideas panned out, leaving us without a way to recreate the two-family experience we missed.

Then, in August 2024, Massachusetts enacted a new law to encourage homeowners to build accessory dwelling units (ADUs), or in-law apartments, to ease the state’s housing shortage. These secondary, self-contained living spaces, complete with kitchens and bathrooms, can house extended family members or paying tenants.

My wife and I immediately knew this could be the solution we’d been looking for. Instead of moving to a two-family home, we could add a small apartment to our existing home. We considered our options and decided that converting a portion of our house into a one-bedroom apartment was the most cost-effective.

We researched town and state ordinances and building codes, then applied for a building permit and submitted plans for the proposed project. Because we weren’t changing the footprint of our home, the process went very smoothly. We started the work in August and had everything completed and inspected by December 2024. We received a certificate of occupancy from the town, and our first tenant moved in on January 1, 2025.

Nearly two years later, we have absolutely no regrets about our ADU conversion project. The rental income has been a fantastic addition to our monthly budget, and we’ve had amazing tenants from the start. It has been the missing piece of our dream home and is making a more secure financial future possible for our family.

If you’re considering adding an ADU to your home or property, here are a few things to keep in mind:

While we had been happy in a two-family home, we mistakenly thought we could do better. But after moving into what was supposed to be our perfect, single-family home, we realized we had made a mistake. Our “dream” house began to feel like a financial burden that only sucked up money and never gave anything back. Staying put and adding a small apartment has given us so much more breathing room and transformed our forever home from a burden into a boon.

#7851. We Tested Ryobi’s $129 Pressure Washer — Here’s What It Can (and Can’t) Do

Can this portable power washer possibly compare to the real thing? We put it to the test.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Nothing sets you up for a better spring than taking some time for some seasonal cleaning in the fall, and one of the best tools for autumn home cleanup is a classic pressure washer. If you’ve got a surface or a screen you need sprayed, a pressure washer can deliver enough pressure for all kinds of scrubbing.

But even the most avid pressure washer advocates would tell you they’re also pretty cumbersome tools that require a lot of setup and garage storage space. That’s exactly why I wanted to try out this portable pressurized washer from Ryobi. The concept is intriguing, promising users a fraction of the size, cost and power of a standard pressure washer. I was very curious whether this tool would actually provide more cleaning power than a standard garden hose nozzle.

The first thing I noticed when unboxing the Ryobi One Plus Electric Power Cleaner was how substantial the tool felt. I was expecting it to feel a little flimsy, but the tool felt well-built in my hands. It all assembled easily in just a few clicks, taking only a small fraction of the time it would’ve taken to set up a full-size pressure washer. And if you’re worried about water ruining your battery, don’t be. The entire battery chamber is enclosed by a tightly sealed plastic housing.

For this test, I decided to replicate a classic fall cleanup task: hosing down screens. I wanted a big surface to clean, so I pulled the screen door off the back door and set it up in the backyard. Then, I applied a light coating of flour to the middle of the screen and a light mist of water to lock the flour in place.

From there, I just had to finish setting up the Ryobi pressure washer. It comes with three different nozzles: two flat angled nozzles and one “turbo nozzle” that sprays the water in a speedy spiral. All I had to do was attach the pressure washer to a garden hose, and the tool was ready to go. Then I just set myself up in front of the screen with the pressure washer the recommended distance (1-2 feet) from the screen. ‘

All that was left to do was let it rip. The first thing that stands out when you use this portable pressure washer is that it feels a little underwhelming when you pull the trigger- especially if you’ve ever used a full-sized pressure washer. There’s not much kick, and the water leaves the nozzle at a steady but uninspiring speed. For a few seconds, I was worried the 700psi of pressure wouldn’t be enough to clean up the floury mess I’d created.

But my worries lessened the longer I used the tool. It was gentler than the pressure washers I’d used before, but it provided a consistent stream that quickly started knocking the flour loose from the screen. Things started going even better once I switched to the turbo nozzle. The spin action really helped compensate for the lack of PSI pressure. Within another minute, I had knocked off a ton of the sticky flour from the screen.

A post shared by Family Handyman (@familyhandyman)

So enough waffling… what’s the verdict? It’s pretty clear, as soon as you start using this tool, that the Ryobi tool isn’t going to fully replace a full-sized pressure washer… especially if you need to really blast something. But there are many use cases for a pressure washer where consistency is more important than power. And if you’ve ever accidentally damaged something with a pressure washer, the reduced power of this tool might even be something you consider a pro.

It took a while, but eventually the screen was sparkling clean- so clean, in fact, it was nearly invisible in the doorway. I should also point out that real-world conditions are rarely as messy as the sticky flour mess I created. If you just need to get dust off a screen or mud off a sidewalk, this tool is a significant upgrade over a simple stream from a garden hose. Ultimately, you’re trading power for portability, and whether that works for you will depend on the job you have to tackle. If it’s only needed for routine seasonal cleaning, this pressure washer could be perfect for you.

Just don’t expect it to peel paint off a pole.

#7850. Prosecution Over Threat to American Federation of Teachers President Randi Weingarten Can Go Forward

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From U.S. v. Spitzer (N.D. Ga.), filed by Magistrate Judge John Larkins on Oct. 9, and just affirmed Wednesday by Judge Eleanor Ross:

The indictment alleges that on July 23, 2024, Mr. Spitzer posted the following message on the website for the American Federation of Teachers, a labor union, regarding its president ("Individual #1"):

[Individual #1] is an ignorant incompetent cunt that should be worried for her safety. Fact that she is still alive. Liberal nazi deserves the bullet to head. Resign before she ends like what happened to trump at his speech. They won't miss fat bitch.

The indictment alleges that the post violated 18 U.S.C. § 875(c), which makes it a federal crime to transmit in interstate commerce any communication containing a threat to injure another person.

Mr. Spitzer argues that assuming the allegations in the indictment were true, it fails to state an offense because the posting was not a "true threat," or even a threat at all, and thus is protected by the First Amendment. As he sees it, the posting was simply political speech about a public figure and did not advocate the use of force or violence against Individual #1.

{In an effort to contextualize the posting, Mr. Spitzer points to an internet article in which Mike Pompeo, the former U.S. Secretary of State, described Individual #1 as "the most dangerous person in the world"; examples of "conservative politicians and commentators" criticizing her approach to school closures during the pandemic; and examples of Individual #1's own political statements. But these are not facts that the Court can consider at this juncture because they fall outside the four corners of the indictment.}

The government responds that whether Mr. Spitzer's posting qualified as a true threat is a question for the jury and that a pretrial determination of the sufficiency of the evidence is procedurally improper. The government further asserts that Mr. Spitzer improperly relies on facts not alleged in the indictment to contextualize the posting. The government has the better argument….

Considering the allegations on the face of the indictment—as this Court must—the Court finds that a jury could conclude that Mr. Spitzer's alleged posting constituted a "true threat." There are at least four separate references to harming or killing Individual #1, including: that she should be "worried for her safety"; that she "deserves a bullet to [the] head"; that unless she resigns she risks being shot similar to the attempted assassination of President Donald J. Trump; and that she will not be missed. In addition, the posting makes an oblique reference to her still being alive, which when combined with the other statements, can reasonably be interpreted as evidencing a present intent to intimidate and place Individual #1 in fear of bodily harm or death. The screed's liberal use of epithets further tends to show that the posting was not simply on a matter of public concern, but rather a threat against Individual #1 personally….

In his reply, Mr. Spitzer relies on the Supreme Court's decision in Watts v. United States, to argue that "political hyperbole" is not a "true threat." True enough, but Watts is distinguishable. In that case, the Supreme Court overturned the conviction of Watts, an 18-year-old Black protester who was charged with threatening President Lyndon B. Johnson during a political rally at the Washington Monument during the 1960's. During the protest, Watts said:

They always holler at us to get an education. And now I have already received my draft classification as 1-A and I have got to report for my physical this Monday coming. I am not going. If they ever make me carry a rifle the first man I want to get in my sights is L.B.J. They are not going to make me kill my black brothers.

The Supreme Court held that considering the full context of the statement—including that it was conditional upon Watt's joining the military (which he said he would not do) and that the listeners laughed at his statement—it was "political hyperbole," not a true threat. In contrast, Mr. Spitzer's alleged statement is much more threatening for the reasons explained above. Also, significantly, Watts was decided after trial, based on a developed evidentiary record, which underscores why dismissal at this juncture is not appropriate.

Accordingly, dismissal of the indictment is not warranted. But, of course, Mr. Spitzer is free to renew his challenge to the sufficiency of the evidence at trial….

Brent A. Gray and Eric John White represent the government.

#7849. Wolverine Loader II Review: No Break-In, No Blisters

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Published Nov 6, 2026 1:24 PM EST

New work boots can be miserable until they’re broken in, especially if you spend long days on your feet. My husband, a contractor who also works on our farm, tested the Wolverine Loader II HyperRest CarbonMAX boots for a full week, wearing them up to 10 hours a day. We had previously tested two of Wolverine’s Infinity System work boots, so we were curious to compare them with this pair’s comfort design. Here’s what we found. (And for more options, see our team-tested best work boots guide.)

The break-in was the biggest surprise of our test. My husband put the Wolverine Loader II boots on and went straight to work. There was no period of stiff leather rubbing against his ankles, no uncomfortable pressure around his toes, and no need to alternate with an older pair while the new boots softened up.

He wore them for a week while doing his regular contracting work and handling chores on our farm, including clearing trees and operating equipment. Some days stretched to 10 hours, but he never complained about sore feet afterward.

Wolverine credits much of that comfort to its (removable) HyperRest footbed, which cushions and supports the foot, and a polyurethane midsole that helps absorb the impact of walking on hard surfaces. The padded collar also helps prevent rubbing around the ankle. Whatever the combination, it worked well for him from the first day.

In our testing, yes. My husband is accustomed to wearing work boots, so he knows the difference between a pair that feels good in the store and one that remains comfortable through a full shift.

The Loader II passed that test. He especially liked how light they felt for boots with protective toes. Wolverine lists the weight at 2.04 pounds per boot, and the CarbonMAX composite toe provides impact and compression protection without the bulk of a traditional steel toe.

The rubber wedge outsole is another feature of the comfort design. Its broad contact area helps distribute weight on hard, flat surfaces, which can be particularly helpful for contractors who spend hours on concrete or other unforgiving flooring.

The Wolverine Loader II is more than just a comfortable boot. Its CarbonMAX toe meets ASTM F2413-24 impact and compression requirements, and the boot also carries electrical hazard and slip-resistance ratings.

The waterproof full-grain leather upper includes reinforced toe and heel bumpers, which help protect areas that often take a beating around tools, equipment, and construction materials. A breathable waterproof membrane and moisture-wicking lining provide additional protection in wet conditions.

Wolverine also uses Goodyear welt construction, which allows the boots to be resoled rather than discarded when the outsole wears out. That’s a welcome feature in a work boot intended for regular use.

One consideration is the wedge outsole. While it’s designed for dependable traction, its relatively flat profile didn’t dig into deep mud as aggressively as some heavily lugged soles. For workers who spend most of their time in muddy fields or on steep, loose terrain, outsole design deserves extra attention.

At $169.95, the Loader II is cheaper than the premium Wolverine Infinity System boots we previously tested, yet it delivered the comfort my husband needs for long workdays.

I think these boots are particularly well suited to contractors, carpenters, equipment operators, and other tradespeople who want safety-toe protection without stiff, heavy footwear. The 6-inch lace-up design also provides a more adjustable fit than a pull-on boot.

After a week of demanding use, my husband had no complaints about comfort, fit, or foot fatigue. That’s an excellent start, although we’ll need more time to judge how the leather, stitching, and outsole hold up over months of daily wear.

For workers who dread breaking in a new pair of boots, the Loader II might just be the ticket.

Whether you’re shopping for a new homeowner or a serious hobbyist, we’ve got a gift idea for you.

#7848. How Old Is Too Old To Use a Chainsaw?

Understand the risks associated with operating a chainsaw as you age with expert-backed advice and safety tips.

While you may take great pride in your ability to take care of things around the house, be careful when it comes to using a chainsaw as you age. Unlike other powered lawn equipment, chainsaws carry a significant risk of personal injury— and can be deadly in the wrong hands.

Ahead, learn how to evaluate when you may be too old to operate a chainsaw and should call in a pro instead, with help from physical therapist Dr. Ron Miller and manual therapist Doug Bertram.

Chainsaw injuries can happen in a fraction of a second and are often due to losing control of the saw during operation. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reports roughly 36,000 chainsaw injuries each year, resulting in serious lacerations, traumatic brain injuries, limb loss or death.

While chainsaws are dangerous to operate at any age, the risks are even higher for older adults. “As we grow older, our ability to control our balance, grip strength, reflex times, eyesight and physical stamina dramatically decreases,” Miller says. “This makes it difficult to operate chainsaws.” It’s crucial that you have the strength and stamina to handle a chainsaw in all conditions to avoid injury.

If you’re not ready to put down the saw yet, consider these tips to do it safely.

Cut smaller logs and branches that are safely on the ground and avoid cutting while on a ladder or felling trees. Hire larger jobs out rather than tackling them yourself.

Consider using a lightweight, electric saw that is easier to control. Regardless of the saw, always make sure the chain is sharp and properly tightened before use.

Wear protective gear: Wearing eye and hearing protection, gloves and sturdy footwear is always sound advice, but don’t overlook chaps too, Miller says. Worn over pants and designed to stop a chainsaw chain, chaps can be the difference between a fatal injury and a superficial wound.

Never cut alone: Always have a cutting partner who remains nearby to help identify dangerous situations and call for help in the event of an accident.

Avoid working to fatigue: “Take breaks to stay awake and alert while operating a chainsaw,” Miller says. Stay well hydrated and fueled to keep your mind sharp during operation and stop when you start to feel tired.

“There’s no age that makes you too old to use a chainsaw,” Bertram says. “[But] you need adequate grip strength, adequate balance and good mental acuity.” It’s less about a specific number and more about your general health and ability. Conduct these physical fitness tests at home to gauge your grip strength, balance, leg and back strength, coordination and endurance. How you perform on these tests will give you a good idea of your functional fitness levels and whether handling a chainsaw is a good idea or not.  When in doubt, hire a pro.

For smaller limbs and logs up to 12-in. in diameter, a bow saw or reciprocating saw with a pruning blade are lower risk options.

Federal law prohibits anyone under the age of 18 from operating a chainsaw in a work setting, but there are no age limits for private chainsaw use on a residential property.

#7847. 16 Types of Blinds Every Homeowner Should Know

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Updated Nov 6, 2026 1:46 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

If you’ve weighed the benefits of curtains, shutters, and blinds in your search for the right window coverings for your home and you’ve settled on blinds, you’re in good company. According to a study by research firm Market Research Future, the size of the window blind market was an estimated $75.48 billion in 2025, and it’s expected to grow to $136.35 billion by 2035. Another research firm, Global Market Insights, found that blinds and shades dominated the window treatment industry in 2025.

With so many different types of blinds on the market, how do you decide which will suit your home best? Whether you’re looking for something sleek and modern or traditional and classic, this guide will help you figure out which ones might be the right pick for your windows.

Blinds are a type of window covering composed of numerous slats, vertical or horizontal, that can be tilted or rotated to adjust the amount of light entering a space. Blinds made of aluminum or vinyl are typically the most cost-efficient types, but there also are blinds crafted of fabric and wood.

They can be installed inside the window frame or above it. Window blinds are typically mounted with specially designed brackets that are sold with the blinds.

The slats are suspended from a track that runs along the top of a window frame. This style of blinds collects less dust than other types of blinds and is easy to clean. The slats just need to be wiped down with a damp cloth.

Best For: Affordability and minimal maintenance

Blinds.com’s vertical blinds are textured, available in a variety of colors, and are guaranteed to fit.

The Home Decorators faux wood Venetian blinds are cordless, making them safe for households with pets or young children.

Mini blinds are like Venetian blinds, with some minor differences. Like Venetian blinds, they are typically made from aluminum or vinyl instead of wood or bamboo. Mini blinds’ slats, however, are usually an inch wide or narrower. While these two types of blinds perform the same way, mini blinds have a sleeker design and thus tend to look more modern and contemporary.

With a minimalist design and cordless operation, the Achim mini blinds are safe and stylish.

Because vinyl blinds are made from PVC and other synthetic materials, they’re a great choice for bathrooms, kitchens, and other areas prone to moisture and humidity. They’re very easy to clean with a cloth or a vacuum attachment. If you’re looking for a window treatment that helps insulate your windows or provides soundproofing, vinyl isn’t your best bet. Still, they are a lot cheaper than wood and other options, if you’re on a budget.

Best For: Budget-conscious shoppers; moisture-prone rooms

Ideal for high-humidity spaces like garages and bathrooms, Bali’s 2-inch vinyl blinds resist chipping and warping and come in dozens of colors.

Wood blinds are a popular choice for those looking to add an element of luxury to their window treatments since wood blinds offer a natural, timeless look that never goes out of style. Not only do they exude sophistication, but they are also incredibly durable and can last for many years with proper care and maintenance. They can be painted or stained to match any color palette, and different slat sizes are available to accommodate shoppers’ specific needs. Wooden blinds tend to be horizontal—or Venetian—style, though vertical wooden blinds are also available.

Best For: Homeowners who are in it for the long haul—these are built to last

Levolor’s 2-inch wood blinds have cordless lift and wand tilt and come in a variety of wood stains.

Sometimes you want the timeless look of a wood blind but don’t have the budget for it. Enter the faux wood blind, which is usually made from PVC or a wood/synthetic blend. Faux wood blinds look like the real deal (though your mileage may vary when it comes to how authentic the wood grain looks), at a fraction of the price. The best part? They can be installed in high-humidity spaces like laundry rooms and bathrooms, where natural wood blinds would mold and warp.

Best for: Budget-conscious homeowners who want a timeless look

Blinds.com’s faux wood blinds are moisture resistant, and available in a variety of wood stains and painted colors.

Aluminum blinds are one of the most popular types of window blinds because of their affordable price and lightweight yet durable design. A sleek, modern look that can complement many decor styles, they are easy to install and incredibly long-lasting. Aluminum blinds also come in a variety of colors, sizes, and textures, allowing homeowners to customize the look of their windows to suit many different aesthetics. In terms of energy efficiency, aluminum blinds help keep a home’s interior cooler by reflecting the sun’s rays away from the window. This helps reduce air conditioning costs since less energy is required to maintain steady temperatures inside the house.

Best For: Easy installation and durability

Sleek and affordable, Blinds.com’s 8-gauge aluminum blinds are available in a variety of neutral colors.

If you’re looking for blinds to cover sliding doors or large windows, consider panel blinds. These window treatments are composed of several panels affixed to a headrail at the top of the window. Each panel is attached to a carrier that slides along a track in order to open or close the blinds. They offer a unique look that differs from standard vertical blinds, making them a great choice for design-forward shoppers.

Roller blinds are technically a type of window shade. An alternative to curtains, these shades are made up of a single piece of fabric material that rolls up and down to control the amount of sunlight that enters the space. Roller shades can be made from a variety of fabrics, ranging from sheer materials to opaque options. While roller blinds might have a reputation for being low quality and not performing well, their design has actually come a long way in recent years.

Chicology’s blackout roller shade has a cordless design and is made from hypoallergenic polyester that won’t attract dust.

UNISHASDES bamboo blinds  partially filter sunlight and come in a variety of sizes and finishes.

Motorized blinds are modern window coverings that you can open and close using a remote control, phone app, or via voice command. Some models have light sensors that automate the opening and closing of your blinds at certain times of the day. Unlike traditional blinds that are adjusted manually, motorized blinds have electric or battery-powered motors that raise and lower them. If you want to be able to control the lighting in a room without ever having to leave your seat, opt for blinds with this feature.

Custom Home Collection’s wood blinds come in over 100 colors and a motorized lift option, which is ideal for smart homes and hard-to-reach windows.

Coolaroo’s knitted HDPE roller shades are mold resistant and block 90 percent of UV rays. Read the review.

Our Recommendation: Coolaroo Exterior Roller Shade at Amazon, priced from $35.25.This exterior window treatment is affordable, cordless, protects against UV rays, and comes in a wide range of finishes.

Sometimes called layered or dual shades, zebra blinds consist of two layers of fabric, each with alternating horizontal bands of sheer and opaque fabric. You can adjust, or roll, the fabric to line up the stripes on the two layers of fabric, meaning opaque is lined up with opaque, and sheer with sheer; this allows light to enter. If you roll the shade such that the opaque stripes on one layer are lined up with the sheer strips on the other layer, the effect is that of an opaque shade, and no light comes through.

Chicology’s zebra blinds are cordless (and thus kid-friendly), light-filtering, and come in three colors.

Also called cellular blinds or cellular shades, honeycomb blinds are constructed of two sheets of fabric that are seamed together horizontally at regular intervals. When looking at these blinds from the side, the resulting pattern somewhat resembles that of a honeycomb. Highly insulating, the design is considered one of the most energy-efficient, and the cellular construction is also good at noise cancellation

Best For: Energy efficiency; homes with a modern vibe

Noise-dampening, cordless, and energy-efficient, the BlindsAvenue honeycomb blinds can be mounted inside or outside the window.

Pleated blinds are made from a single length of woven fabric that is pressed into sharp, horizontal pleats at regular intervals, yielding a zig-zag appearance. The blind is raised or lowered to adjust the amount of light entering the room. While they’re often compared to honeycomb blinds, pleated blinds don’t offer the same insulating properties as cellular blinds. Pleated blinds offer a clean, modern look.

Best For: Decorators in search of an elegant, minimalist look.

Semi-sheer and cordless, these pull-down blinds from Calyx Interiors are available in four colors and several sizes.

Best For: Rooms in which someone needs to sleep during the day.

These cordless, pull-down blackout blinds from Persilux are available in five colors and multiple sizes.

Our Recommendation: Persilux Custom, Cordless Blackout Cellular Blinds at Amazon starting at $63.99. These cordless, pull-down blinds are available in five colors and numerous sizes.

#7846. 4 Common Tools With a Hidden Second Function Most People Never Use

Some everyday tools hide useful features in plain sight. These four have built-in cutters, openers, and other functions worth knowing about.

A pair of pliers can sit in the same toolbox for years without its owner ever noticing the cutting edge near the hinge. The same goes for measuring tools, utility knives, and even gadgets in a kitchen drawer.

Some everyday tools have other tools built in, but those extra features are easy to overlook. Anyone who has spent time on home improvement projects knows how frustrating it can be to search for a tool, especially when the one already in hand could do the job.

Of course, features vary by model, but these four familiar tools have some useful extras worth knowing about.

Some pliers have built-in wire cutters near the hinge, just behind the gripping jaws. These can trim soft wire without needing a separate pair of cutters. Not every pair has this feature, though. It’s also worth checking whether the tool has wire strippers, which remove insulation without cutting through the wire itself.

Some wire strippers have small, threaded holes near the handles that allow users to shorten machine screws. The screw goes into the appropriately sized hole, and squeezing the handles cuts it to length. This feature can come in handy when installing electrical fixtures or other hardware that requires shorter screws.

Some manual can openers have a bottle opener built into the handle or near the cutting mechanism. Depending on the design, it may look like a small notch or hook in the metal. Other models have magnets that help lift cut lids from cans without touching the sharp edges.

Many nail clippers have a small metal file that folds out from beneath the lever or sits along the body. It helps smooth rough edges after trimming. Some models also have a pointed tip for cleaning beneath nails, although the design and placement of these extra features vary.
